title: On service
hookLine: he warns against service mixed with pride
last: THE GURU'S LIGHT SHOWS THE WAY.

cards: A bundle of grass, cut for the cattle, soaking wet and caked with mud. Someone has to carry it home on their head. In the story Sikhs tell, Guru Nanak asks who will take it.
His sons have reasons not to. Then a newer disciple, a man named Lehna, dressed in fine clothes, lifts the dripping bundle onto his own head. Mud runs down his face and into the cloth.
He carries it anyway. Lehna would become Guru Angad. And when he wrote about service, he warned about a quieter danger, the one that can ride along on any good deed.

teach.b: In Asa di Var, the morning ballad, there's a salok marked Mahala two, Guru Angad's voice. In paraphrase: a servant who serves with pride, and argues while he does it, and talks on and on, does not win the Master's favor.
But one who loses himself and serves is given some honor. Nanak, he meets the One he is devoted to, and his devotion is accepted. Look at the three things it names: pride, arguing, talking too much.
None of them stop the work.
The dishes still get washed, the floor still gets swept. The problem is what rides along on top. Pride says, look who's helping.
Arguing says, I'd do it differently and you should know. Talking says, let me tell you what this cost me. Each one turns service back toward the self.
The second half is plain: lose yourself and serve. Not lose the work; lose the self in it. Then honor comes, not from the people watching but from the Master.
In Sikh life this is seva: cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, cleaning shoes at the gurdwara door. And the Lehna story fits the salok exactly. He made no speech about the muddy grass.
He didn't mention his ruined clothes.

how: Sikhs practice seva, selfless service, in the gurdwara and beyond: cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, cleaning, and looking after the shoes of the sangat, ideally without seeking notice.

o: service that earns honor from the people watching
service done only inside the gurdwara walls
serving with the self left out: no pride, no fuss

games.q: service in the salok and the story: tap the pairs.

s: in the salok, the proud servant stops doing the work
the work still gets done; the problem is the pride, arguing and talk riding on top of it.
the salok says the one who loses himself and serves is given honor
and his devotion is accepted, it says.
Lehna, in the story, is the man who became Guru Angad
the disciple who carried the muddy bundle later became the second Guru.

games.q: you're in your best clothes. your teacher asks who will carry a dripping bundle of muddy grass home on their head. what does Lehna do?
o: lifts it onto his own head and carries it.
carries it, then points out his ruined clothes.
games.why: the story says he carried it, mud running down, and said nothing about the clothes: service with the self left out.

practice: Picture one small service you'll do today, for family, a coworker, a stranger, and notice which of the three would most like to come along: the pride, the arguing, or the telling everyone afterward.
Don't scold it; just see it, and picture setting it down at the door before you go in. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: On service. Guru Angad's warning: service done with pride, arguing and too much talk loses its way; lose yourself and serve, and it is accepted. Today's word.

orig.note: seva: selfless service, the work Guru Angad's salok asks to be done without pride.

carryVoice: Your line: serve plainly. The work is enough, without the story about it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Asa di Var, salok Mahala 2, Ang 474 (the servant who serves with pride and argument; lose yourself and serve)
Janamsakhi tradition: Lehna carries the bundle of wet grass
